Any easy way to do so? Platform is not a problem, I can do Windows 7, Mac, Linux.
Is there any way to extract individual episodes from a DVD of TVs, naming each episode properly?

hi DerKatalog! I'm a little late to the party, but this question is right up my alley. I've ripped hundreds of TV shows and thousands of movies from my DVD collection into my Plex server to stream across my LAN. The three programs I'd recommend are MakeMKV, Handbrake, and Plex.

MakeMKV (free while in beta) will rip DVDs and Blu Rays into an .mkv format. For movies this is pretty straightforward. For TV shows, you'll usually see 4 or 5 titles per disc that are already divided into episodes, ready to rename.

Handbrake (free, open source) takes a bit of tinkering, but it will convert the MKVs that you get from the discs into a much lighter and more modern mp4/m4v format, perfect for storing and streaming.

Plex is the holy grail of LAN streaming. It's free to use for LAN (subscription fee if you want to stream your server's content across the internet.) It'll run on the average desktop just fine and has client apps for Roku, Android, chromecast, and pretty much everything. It will even transcode as you stream into whatever format your clients support. The server software will download metadata for your TV shows and movies and present them in a Netflix-like format. For someone with a low bandwidth cap and a big DVD collection, it's pretty darn sweet.

Edit: all three are Linux compatible, with .deb and .rpm packages available.

I would add one more item to ChillyHellion's equation, Filebot for bulk file renames.

For episodes I like the format:

/cleaned/{n}/{'Season '+s.pad(2)/{n}.{s00e00}.t.{vc}.{vf}

And for movies: 

/cleaned/{n} {[y]}.{vc}.{vf}

edit If you need a bulk file renaming application for Windows I'd recommend Bulk File Renamer The interface is a cluster-F* but it's powerful once you get used to it.

You are tracked this way on half of all sites even if not explicitly attempted. Not every site uses this format but if you give every visitor a session cookie and then when they login in associate that session cookie with a user then when they logout don't clear that session cookie but just the association. If you are logging page views against that cookie and also username you can easily put two and two together after the fact.

A lot of companies do this not to track people after they log out but instead before they log in. That way if there is a registration process you can look at what they were doing before they registered and tie that to a user and tie that to other behavior to try to understand them.

If Reddit writes scripts after the fact that utilizes that data then that's tracking after you've logged out. Undoubtedly reddit would get around to writing that script at somepoint. The other useful thing that does is help associate alts. So now imagine the police take some interest in hate speech. The data is there to get the alt so the police can demand it whether reddit had hoped to ever tie that data together or not. Now your other accounts have some identifiable information or you've used the psuedonym on another site and that might be your gmail or youtube (which ties to gmail) or amazon account. Get a gmail you know their phone if it's android.

There's no reason you wouldn't do the session cookies this way because it gives useful data. I do it as a knee jerk method because I never know when data might be useful if a project grows. The cookies have to be implemented some way, why not that way.
